# Editor Scope

## How To Build

A EditorScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A EditorScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

An editor for a file opened from the [FileTreeScope](../../ui/components/file-tree/index.md#file-tree-scope), or anywhere else the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, with language support for Piton files.

### Shape

#### Description

Editable and syntax highlighted, in its own tab of the [BodyScope](../application/Body.md#body-scope), under a header with the file's path in the project, a dot while it has unsaved changes, a save button, and a close button.

#### Syntax Highlighting

Every file is highlighted in its language, using the grammars gpui-kit's editor comes with: Piton, and Astro, Bash, C, C++, C#, CMake, CSS, diffs, EJS, Elixir, ERB, Go, GraphQL, HTML, Java, JavaScript, JSON, Kotlin, Lua, Make, Markdown, PHP, Protocol Buffers, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, Svelte, Swift, TOML, TSX, TypeScript, YAML, and Zig. SQL is left out, as its grammar can't be built alongside gpui.
The language comes from the file's extension, ignoring case, including the other extensions a language goes by, such as .h for C, .hpp and .cc for C++, .jsx, .mjs, and .cjs for JavaScript, .mts and .cts for TypeScript, .htm for HTML, .exs for Elixir, .zsh for Bash, .yml for YAML, and .scss, .sass, and .less for CSS. Some files are known by their whole name instead: Makefile for Make, CMakeLists.txt for CMake, Cargo.lock for TOML, Gemfile and Rakefile for Ruby, and shell startup files like .bashrc and .zshrc for Bash. A file in any other language, or with no extension, is plain text.

#### Selecting Text

Selecting text in the editor by dragging across it shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../ui/components/selection-popover/index.md#selection-popover-scope) with four buttons:

- Cut, with a scissors icon, which puts the selected text on the clipboard and removes it from the file
- Copy, with a copy icon, which puts the selected text on the clipboard
- Paste, with a clipboard icon, which puts what is on the clipboard in place of the selected text
- Send to Prompt, with a paperclip icon, which attaches the selected text to the prompt, as attaching text selected in an answer does

Cut, Copy, and Paste do just what their shortcuts do in the editor, and can be undone the same way. Cut and Paste are disabled while the file can't be edited yet. After any of them the editor keeps focus. The popover also closes when the text changes, or when the file closes.

#### Ruler

A thin vertical line, in the theme's line colour, runs down the text at the 80th column, the width a line should keep within. Past it, the editor's background is a step darker than the well, as black laid over it, 25% in dark mode and 5% in light mode, so text running long stands out while staying as readable. The line and the shade scroll sideways with the text, are drawn behind it, and never take the mouse.

#### Keyboard

##### Indentation

A tab stop is 4 spaces: <Tab> indents by 4 spaces, <Shift+Tab> outdents by 4, and a new line's indentation counts in 4s.

##### Backspace

<Backspace> with nothing selected, when everything between the start of the line and the cursor is spaces, deletes back to the tab stop before the cursor, up to 4 spaces at once, as though the indentation were tabs. Anywhere else, or with a selection, it deletes as ever, a character or the selection.

##### Home

The editor moves about a line the way a good code editor does. <Home> goes to the line's first character that isn't whitespace; pressed again there, or on a line that is only whitespace, it goes to the very start of the line, and pressed again from there, back to its first character. With <Shift> it selects the same way.

##### New Lines

<Enter> starts the new line at the indentation of the line it breaks, as the language's indentation rules say. On a line that is an item of a Markdown or Piton list, starting with a dash, an asterisk, or a plus and a space, or a number and a period and a space, the new line starts a new item of the same list at the same indentation, a numbered item counting on from the one before. <Enter> on an item with nothing after its marker ends the list

###### Instead

the marker is taken away, leaving the line empty at its

indentation. <Enter> with an open completion or quick fix menu is the menu's.

#### New Files

The editor can also show a file that isn't on disk yet, starting with the text it is given. It has unsaved changes from the start, and saving it writes it, making its folders as needed.

#### Saving

Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) or the save button writes the file to disk. A file that cannot be saved keeps its changes and says why beneath the header.
Saving never moves the cursor or the view. A Piton file is formatted as it is saved, and the editor then shows the formatted text, with the cursor still at the same place in the text, beside the same characters it was beside, and scrolled just as it was.

#### Language Support

```
overview: A Piton file (`.pi`) is edited with the project's [LSP](../lsp/index.md#lsp) server, shared with the chat input, which sees the editor's unsaved text: the file is opened with `textDocument/didOpen`, kept current with full-text `textDocument/didChange`, reported with `textDocument/didSave` when saved, and closed with `textDocument/didClose` when the editor closes or shows another file. Other files are edited without language support, as is a Piton file while the server is not running.
completions: `textDocument/completion` is requested after typing a letter, a digit, an opening curly brace, a period, a dollar sign, an at sign, a colon, or an underscore, and narrowed and ordered as in the chat input. Accepting a completion also applies the import the server attaches to it.
hover: Hovering a name shows the server's `textDocument/hover`. Typing in the editor clears whatever the pointer's hover shows, the name's hover and a diagnostic's message alike, as soon as a key changes the text, and nothing hovered shows again until the pointer next moves over the text.
definitions: Ctrl-clicking (Cmd-clicking on macOS) a name goes to its `textDocument/definition`. A definition in another file opens that file at the definition, as the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says.
diagnostics: What the server publishes for the file is underlined, with the message shown on hover, and kept while the text is edited until the server publishes again.
quickFixes: Ctrl+. (Cmd+. on macOS) lists the server's `textDocument/codeAction` fixes at the cursor, and picking one applies its edits to the file.
```

#### Other Files

Each open file has an editor of its own. Opening another file opens it in another tab, leaving this one as it is, its unsaved changes, cursor, and scrolling kept for when its tab is selected again.

#### Closing

The close button above the file, or the one on its tab, closes it. While there are unsaved changes, it first asks whether to discard them.

# Chat Input Scope

## How To Build

A ChatInputScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A ChatInputScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well as snippets of Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
The body beneath the tabs has 8 pixels of padding. In it, the text input sits in a dark box on the theme's darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, with rounded corners and no border, as tall as the column of buttons beside it, 8 pixels from it, and taller when its text needs more. The text sits 8 pixels in from the box's top, left, and right, and grows down through the box. Clicking anywhere in the box beneath the text puts focus in the text, except while a preview shows. The preview shows in the same box, its content inset 8 pixels all round.
At the right, a column of three buttons, 120 pixels wide, 6 pixels apart, each as tall as the input's single row: Send at the top, then Queue, then Preview, each the column's full width. Send has a send icon before its label, and keeps its split chevron, the send menu staying the only way to reach "Send to task". Queue and Preview are buttons in gpui-kit's default style, doing what the send menu's options of those names do, with tooltips saying that Queue queues the prompt even while the harness is free, and that Preview previews the compiled prompt. They are offered just as the menu is: both are disabled while the input is empty, while a preview shows, and while a queued prompt is edited, and Queue is also disabled on the Ask tab, since a question never queues.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegrationScope
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. While the harness is working, the send button on the Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

#### Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInput.md#chat-input-instruction)

#### Send Options

##### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

##### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.

##### Options

The menu's options, in order:

- "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
- "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it
- "Send to task", with a send icon, only while a task is running with a harness that can be fed more, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and its output is shown, the previous tasks not expanded over it; never on the Ask tab, where a question runs on its own. It sends what is typed, and what is attached, to the running task instead of queueing it, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, and clears the input as sending does. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) still queues, as the send button does

#### Editing Queued

Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor), sets aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab, and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text. Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and the send menu isn't offered.
Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it, cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in progress; so does switching projects.

#### Preview

Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with, at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs, attachments, and send button stay as they are.
The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape> goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

#### Tabs

##### Overview

The input and buttons live inside the body of a tab bar, using gpui-kit's default tab styling, except that each tab's label is always in its mode's colour at full strength, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), whether selected or not: Code red, Spec blue, Ask green, and Freeform grey. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, and Freeform. Code, Spec, Ask, and Freeform are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All five sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask to Freeform and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text

###### Either

they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next

or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.

##### Chain

Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
In combined mode, with Chain selected, Chain has no line along its bottom, just as the joined Code and Spec beneath it have none. In separate mode, unselected, it has one, like any other unselected

###### Tab

the tab bar's bottom line runs beneath it, the same colour and

thickness, in the same place, as beneath any other unselected tab, at any display scale. This holds at every window size and display scale, in light and dark mode: in combined mode nothing draws a line beneath Chain at all, rather than a line being drawn and then hidden, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.

##### Help

To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) says.

##### Session

At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New conversation button. The questions of the Ask tab have a conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so the figure is the Ask tab's conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New conversation is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon, reading "New conversation". Pressing it starts a new conversation for the selected tab: the tasks' on Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform, the questions' on Ask. The next run in that tab, or in any tab sharing its conversation, starts a new one with no context instead of carrying on, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back, even once the project is closed and opened again, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

Pressed for the tasks with prompts queued, New conversation marks the first in the queue, saving it again with the project, so it still starts the new conversation once the project is closed and opened again. With nothing queued, the next task sent or queued takes the mark. Cancelling the marked prompt passes the mark on to the one that now comes first, or, with nothing left queued, to the next task sent or queued. Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is the cost of this project's runs since it was opened, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when it reports no cost either. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  its cost.
- This project: the same totals for every run in the project since
  it was opened, tasks and questions, and how many runs there were.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

##### Colour

The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope). With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey; neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they have been given in the theme editor.
The send button, both its halves, takes the same colour as the selected tab, purple with Chain selected, but at full strength rather than as a tint, so it stands out against the tinted body. Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never staying solid across a faded button.

#### System Prompt

The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system prompt is sent with it, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.

#### Ask

Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already running.
Each question's progress and results are shown in a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope). The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and first line.
However many questions are asked, the stack is only as tall as its rows, up to 240 pixels, the queue's most, and scrolls beyond that with a [ScrollbarScope](../../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope), kept on the newest question, nearest the tabs, as each is asked. Once it holds more than fit, the stack lays out only the rows in view, as a table does, so a long stack costs no more to show, scroll, or animate than a short one, and the drawer's bottom follows the stack's top as ever.
Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status and first line, above its full task table, in the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope), which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time: opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

#### Answer Steps

For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer, the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says. A question closed into the previous answers starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list).

#### Previous Answers

Previous answers are a [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope), shown only while the Ask tab is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers", "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded, "Back to the questions". Each previous answer offers Resend, which asks its question again, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Expanded, the row and the list go into the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope), sliding up from on top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

#### Answer Drawer

[AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/index.md#answer-drawer-scope)

#### Selecting Answer Text

The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../../ui/components/selection-popover/index.md#selection-popover-scope) with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The popover also closes when the drawer closes.

#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Images can be attached too: pasted from the clipboard while the chat input has focus, dropped onto the chat input from the file manager, or chosen with a small ghost button with an image icon, whose tooltip says "Attach images", on the tab row between the last tab and the help text, which opens the platform's file picker for any files, several at once, since the picker can't be limited to images. Pasting an image attaches it rather than putting anything in the text, even when the clipboard holds text as well; every image on the clipboard is attached, and a clipboard with no image pastes its text as usual. Several files dropped or chosen at once are attached in their order, each on its own merits. An image is known by its content, not its name, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP are taken: anything else pasted, dropped, or chosen, BMP, TIFF, and SVG included, is not attached, and a warning notification titled "Not attached" says it isn't an image. An image larger than 5 MB is not attached either, and the same notification says it is too large. A folder dropped or chosen isn't an image either, and a file that can't be read is not attached, the same notification saying it couldn't be read, and why. Each file left out has its own notification, and the others are still attached.
Files can be dropped only on the chat input itself, its tabs, the attachments, and the text input; dropping them on the message list above it does nothing. While files are dragged over the chat input, its background is highlighted with the accent's fill, laid about a quarter of the way over it.
An attached image's row shows a small thumbnail, its file name, or "Pasted image" for one pasted, and its size in pixels, muted, with the same remove button; hovering the thumbnail shows the image larger, at most 320 pixels. Images and text are listed together in the order they were attached while the prompt is written. A prompt taken back into the input, as when a queued prompt is edited, lists its text first, then its images, each image named by its saved file, a pasted one included.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Projects

The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous answers belong to their project, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says: switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The prompt being written, its attachments, the selected tab, and the Slice toggle stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

#### Escape

Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat input. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS) brings it back, from anywhere the chat input isn't beneath something else, as the [MainWindowScope](../../application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope) says.

The text input is a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input-scope) growing to 12 rows at most. Its first row lines up with the send button, both at the top of the input row, and it grows downward from there.

```

accepting: Accepting one inserts it as a mention, as the [HarnessCatalogScope](../../harness-integration/catalog/index.md#harness-catalog-scope) says, in place of what was typed of it. Mentions work without the [LSP](../../lsp/index.md#lsp).
```

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope)

##### Escaping

A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes all mean something. The anchor is exported, so that it compiles, and its userPrompt is a multi-line escape block, which Piton keeps exactly as it is: the prompt's lines, each at the block's indentation, fenced by a line of three backslashes, or of one more than any line of the prompt made only of backslashes, so nothing in it closes the block early. The systemPrompt is written the same way.
Each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported, in the userPrompt and then the systemPrompt, is also listed once, in the order they first appear, as an item of the anchor's references property, left out when there are none; a reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. `piton compile` resolves the references. A prompt saved by an earlier version, as quoted pieces or as prose, still reads back.

I added the shortcut: pressing Ctrl+Shift+Up in the chat input now moves focus to the editor of the file whose tab is selected. When the Chat tab is selected there's no active editor, so the chat input keeps focus. The new test for both cases passes. In the full suite, 393 tests pass and 4 fail. All 4 check the system prompt templates, which my change doesn't touch. The one I inspected fails because its expected wording (that reading the spec means following references) no longer matches the template text, so the failures were there before this change.

**What changed**
- `src/chat_input.rs`: a new `FocusEditor` action bound to `ctrl-shift-up` in the chat input. It sends a `FocusActiveEditor` event.
- `src/prompt_mode.rs`: prompt mode listens for that event and focuses the editor in the selected file tab (`focus_open_file`). The new test `ctrl_shift_up_focuses_the_selected_file` is here too.
- `src/file_view.rs`: a small test-only helper, `editor_focused`.

**Things to know**
- **Not in the spec yet:** none of the specs mention Ctrl+Shift+Up, so the understanding file's main constraint links to your prompt file. You may want to add the shortcut to the chat input spec.
- **Ctrl on macOS too:** it's Ctrl+Shift+Up on every platform, as Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+N already are, so it isn't Cmd on macOS. It doesn't clash with the text box's own keys (Cmd+Shift+Up is "select to start" there).
- **Formatter:** I ran `cargo fmt` on the whole project, and several files already had your uncommitted changes. It may have reformatted some of those lines as well.
